MARKETING MATERIAL. Opening frame: What’s driving markets? Market take Camera frame Title slide: Midterms and AI in focus at 2027 Forum We held our Forum as the U.S. midterms unfolded and markets increasingly priced in a supply-driven regime we’ve long described. Attention is now turning from the AI buildout to demand, adoption and who benefits, as competition for capital intensifies. These shifts will help shape our 2027 Global Outlook. 1: An evolving AI story Markets are still working through what the Democratic sweep of Congress means for the AI buildout. The buildout will continue, but the focus is now on whether it will be at the same scale and at the same pace. And whether adoption can keep up. And that was a key discussion at our Forum last week. A slowdown could have significant consequences for markets. But it could also ease competition for capital and bring bond yields down. Much uncertainty remains about the speed and the size of the buildout. And that uncertainty was behind our move to neutral on U.S. equities and our upgrade of U.S. Treasuries last month. 2: Funding in focus Competition for capital was another major focus. The AI buildout is competing for funding with government borrowing, with investment in energy and in defense. And Hyperscalers are still spending heavily, even as financing costs rise. And that raises a key question: Can stronger growth and earnings offset those higher costs, and where will the pressure show up next? 3: Eyeing rates We’ve long expected rates to stay structurally higher. At the forum, the focus was on what that means for markets and portfolios. Shifting capital flows, changing correlations between stocks, bonds and currencies could create new sources of volatility and challenge traditional portfolio hedges. That makes staying flexible key to navigating risks and seizing opportunities. Outro: Here’s our Market take The takeaway from our Forum was that AI adoption and competition for capital are critical from here. These topics will be key for our 2027 Global Outlook published next month. Closing frame: Read details: blackrock.com/weekly-commentary An internal debate At our internal 2027 Forum last week, the U.S. midterms, AI adoption and competition for capital ran through the debates among our portfolio managers. Market backdrop U.S. stocks fell sharply after a brief post-midterm rally, with the Nasdaq entering correction territory as concerns over the AI buildout intensified. Week ahead Following last week's strong U.S. payrolls report, CPI and PPI will offer fresh clues on inflation this week ahead of the Fed's December meeting. The U.S. midterms dominated headlines last week as Democrats took control of Congress. Our 2027 Outlook Forum was consequential given the big unresolved macro questions . The supply-driven regime we’ve described for five years is largely priced in, making the outlook less directional. For AI, attention has shifted from the buildout toward demand, adoption and who benefits as competition for capital intensifies. These debates will shape next month’s 2027 Global Outlook. Nasdaq correction refers to a decline of at least 5% from its previous peak. U.S. stocks rallied the day after the elections, sold off sharply on Thursday and steadied on Friday. See the chart. The swings illustrate a key conclusion from our 2027 Outlook Forum: the AI story is moving into a more nuanced phase. In the initial phase of the AI transformation, the investment opportunity was about pricing the conviction that the buildout needed to happen. Now the focus is shifting to assessing the size and speed of the buildout relative to how quickly AI is adopted and spreads across different tasks. A material slowdown in 2027, though far from certain, could have significant adverse market consequences. But it could also ease competition for capital and lower bond yields, while its economic fallout could temper policy initiatives. This two-sided uncertainty underpinned our move to neutral on U.S. equities and our upgrade of U.S. Treasuries last month. The AI infrastructure boom has been a powerful driver of growth, earnings and market returns. But how long will scarcity persist, and where might abundance emerge as constraints ease? These questions ran through our Forum discussions. Participants debated how much AI capacity will ultimately be built, whether demand from adoption can justify the scale of investment and when opportunities might shift from suppliers to adopters. We heard directly from corporate CFOs about how they are deploying AI and assessing its benefits, offering a window into demand that remains difficult to measure. Another question was what would happen if capital spending slowed before productivity gains from adoption materialized. And who ultimately captures the gains and who gets disrupted – technology providers, businesses adopting AI or their customers? Competition for capital a hot topic Competition for capital was another major topic, as the extraordinary financing needs of AI collide with government borrowing and investment in energy security and defense. Our portfolio managers debated whether this growing demand for funding could crowd out other borrowers, even as AI investment supports economic growth and risk assets. With credit markets becoming more selective, participants also discussed whether greater equity issuance could help hyperscalers manage leverage and preserve their capacity to borrow as the buildout continues. Another key question was whether stronger growth and earnings can continue to offset higher financing costs – and where the pressure might emerge next. The Forum came at a consequential juncture. After four years of an AI-driven bull market, markets have largely priced in the new regime of structurally higher interest rates we’ve talked about for five years. That makes the investment outlook less directional and more nuanced. Discussions ranged from shifting global capital flows and changing relationships between stocks, bonds and currencies to investment opportunities across Europe, China and emerging markets. Participants also explored how evolving market structures could affect market liquidity and volatility. The reliability of traditional portfolio hedges and the importance of retaining flexibility were also major topics. Our bottom line Our 2027 Outlook Forum highlighted the questions facing investors as the supply-driven regime we’ve described for five years becomes increasingly priced in. Look out for more in our 2027 Global Outlook next month. Market backdrop U.S. stocks fell sharply last week following the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections, despite a rebound on Friday. For the week, the Nasdaq 100 lost 4.7%, leaving it 14% below its October peak, while the S&P 500 dropped 2.4%. U.S. Treasuries rallied, with 10-year yields falling 13 basis points over the week to 4.86%. Brent crude fell 17% to $97 a barrel amid hopes for an end to the Middle East conflict. U.S. inflation data take center stage this week, with CPI and PPI offering the latest read on price pressures ahead of the Fed's December policy meeting. We expect persistent inflation pressures to keep market expectations for further Fed rate hikes alive. China's inflation and trade data will shed light on domestic demand and external activity, while UK and euro area GDP figures will provide a snapshot of European growth. Nov. 9 China PPI & CPI Nov.10 U.S. CPI; China trade balance Nov. 12 UK GDP estimate Nov. 13 U.S. PPI; EU GDP & employment flash estimate Intersecting mega forces Since we launched our mega forces framework, it has become clearer how their intersection shapes almost all our investment views and opens up alpha opportunities. They cut across asset class labels, spurring a rethink of portfolio construction. Investors need to be deliberate about the economic or thematic exposures they own, the vehicles they use to implement them and their investment horizons. From drivers to portfolio expressions Our highest conviction views, November 2026 Driver What we think Portfolio expression Growth and AI scarcity AI fundamentals are strong, but we eye near-term volatility. Neutral U.S. equities and overweight EM equities; favor AI- and tech-related opportunities. Duration and diversification Higher starting yields improve prospective returns and income. Overweight short-term U.S. Treasuries for solid income and a cushion against higher rates; neutral long-term Treasuries. Credit spreads and liquidity Selectivity is crucial amid tight spreads and uneven fundamentals. Credit with clear cash flows, lender protections and recovery value; higher-rated high yield. Inflation and scarcity Scarcity, secure supply and power demand carry inflation risks. Infrastructure, energy bottlenecks, EM local debt and real-asset-linked exposures. Alpha opportunity Macro outcomes matter again in the new regime. Macro hedge funds, venture capital, market-neutral strategies, and selected private credit and non-U.S. alpha. Asset class implications Six- to 12-month tactical positioning, November 2026 This shows the implementation of our key investment views from the previous page through an asset class lens. Search views Asset Tactical view Commentary Equities United States We are neutral. Strong AI fundamentals remain supportive, but policy uncertainty could fuel near-term volatility. We continue to favor AI and tech. Europe We are neutral. We would need to see more business-friendly policy and deeper capital markets for Europe to outperform. We favor financials, infrastructure and industrials. UK We are neutral. Valuations remain attractive relative to the U.S., but we see few near-term catalysts to trigger a shift. Japan We are neutral. Strong corporate balance sheets and governance reforms remain supportive. We prefer targeted exposures to physical AI and the buildout’s bottlenecks. Emerging markets (EM) We are overweight. Strong earnings and cheaper valuations create opportunities. We particularly like different expressions of the AI scarcity theme across Asia and Latin America. China We are neutral. We see opportunities in physical AI. Cheap, open-source AI could drive adoption, but that doesn’t necessarily translate into AI-provider profitability. Fixed income Short U.S. Treasuries We are overweight. Much of the repricing we anticipated has occurred, and expectations for further Fed hikes look excessive. We favor the front end for attractive income and a greater breakeven buffer. Long U.S. Treasuries We are neutral. Higher yields offer attractive income and a bigger cushion against further rate increases. We still see room for yields to rise as competition for capital intensifies. Global inflation-linked bonds We are neutral. We see inflation settling above pre-pandemic levels, but markets may not price this in the near term as economic growth could slow. Euro area government bonds We are neutral on short- and medium-term bonds. Current ECB rate pricing looks fairly valued given the balance of risks. Higher energy prices could push rates higher. We prefer to deploy risk elsewhere. UK gilts We are neutral. We expect periods of elevated volatility given political uncertainty, longer-term bonds making up a larger market share, and buyers becoming more price-sensitive. Japanese government bonds We are underweight. The substantial repricing in yields has improved the risk-reward, but further rate hikes and heavy issuance could push yields higher. China government bonds We are neutral. China bonds offer stability and diversification but developed market yields are higher. A shift in investor sentiment toward equities limits upside. U.S. agency MBS We are neutral and lean into the stable income MBS provide despite tight spreads. Short-term IG credit We are neutral. Spreads are tight due to corporate strength, but attractive overall yields help offset the risk of increased issuance. Long-term IG credit We are underweight. We prefer short-term bonds less exposed to interest rate risk over long-term bonds. But attractive overall yields help offset the risk of increased issuance. Global high yield We are neutral. High yield offers attractive income. We prefer higher-rated U.S. and European high yield over investment grade and see dispersion of returns increasing. Asia credit We are neutral. Overall yields are attractive and fundamentals are solid, but spreads are tight. Emerging hard currency We are neutral. Fundamentals have improved, but we see a more attractive risk-reward profile in EM local debt. Emerging local currency We are overweight.
